# Give Data Sync a dedicated GitHub App identity

## Context

The scheduled Data Sync Pipeline is currently failing for more than one reason. A census of its latest 100 runs through 2026-07-23 07:37 UTC found 67 failures and 33 successes. Two authorization boundaries account for 52 of those 67 failures:

- 39 generated-data pushes rejected by the active [`code scanning merge protection` ruleset](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/rules/19087298)
- 13 DevIndex OptIn reads rejected with `Resource not accessible by integration`

Representative evidence: [ruleset rejection](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/actions/runs/29559832086), [current failing run](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/actions/runs/29988762639).

## Problem

The workflow passes the repository-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` through all DevIndex stages, including the cross-repository OptIn read from `neomjs/devindex-opt-in`. It then creates a fresh local commit and pushes it directly to `dev` with the same identity.

These are different authorization contracts, but today they share one token:

1. The repository token is not an explicit cross-repository identity for the OptIn repository.
2. A new generated commit cannot already carry target-branch CodeQL evidence, while the active code-scanning ruleset has no permitted bypass actor for this pipeline.

The retry work in #15359 remains useful for genuinely transient reads. Its conclusion that the current integration denial can be treated as transient is no longer sufficient for this persistent configuration boundary. Closed historical tickets remain immutable; this ticket supersedes only that diagnosis.

## Architectural Reality

- The workflow grants `contents: write`, passes `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` into every data stage, then runs a direct rebase/push sequence: [`data-sync-pipeline.yml`](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/f1a8013b01488e05445888470ad21a439704b230/.github/workflows/data-sync-pipeline.yml#L16-L81).
- OptIn targets a separate repository: [`OptIn.mjs`](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/f1a8013b01488e05445888470ad21a439704b230/apps/devindex/services/OptIn.mjs#L29-L76).
- The GitHub service currently classifies `Resource not accessible by integration` inside its retry path: [`GitHub.mjs`](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/f1a8013b01488e05445888470ad21a439704b230/apps/devindex/services/GitHub.mjs#L325-L434).
- GitHub documents `GITHUB_TOKEN` as scoped to the workflow repository and documents installation-token creation for GitHub Apps in Actions: [token scope](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/github_token), [GitHub App authentication](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/making-authenticated-api-requests-with-a-github-app-in-a-github-actions-workflow).

## Fix

Create **two** dedicated, least-privilege GitHub App identities for Data Sync and install each only on the repositories it must reach.

> **Amended 2026-07-26.** This section originally prescribed **one** App. The two-identity split was raised in @neo-gpt-emmy's intake delta and shipped in PR #15953; the body is corrected here rather than left contradicting the implementation. `actions/create-github-app-token@v3` scopes ONE permission set across a whole repository set, so a single App spanning all three repos would give the ruleset-bypass identity write access to the intake repositories **and** let the intake identity publish to `neo`. For an actor that bypasses a security ruleset, that coupling is the wrong trade.

| Identity | Installed on | Permissions | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Publisher** | `neomjs/neo` | `contents: write` | supplies the checkout/push credential; **sole** ruleset-bypass actor |
| **Intake** | `neomjs/devindex-opt-in`, `neomjs/devindex-opt-out` | `issues: write`, `metadata: read`, explicitly **no** `contents` | injected only into the OptIn/OptOut collection stages |

- Mint short-lived installation tokens near workflow start from each App's credentials.
- Pass each token only to the stages entitled to it — never one token for both boundaries.
- Request the permissions **explicitly** on the token, not only on the installation: without `permission-*` inputs the action mints a token carrying every permission the installation holds, so least-privilege would live in a settings page nobody reads at review time.
- Add that specific App as the code-scanning-ruleset bypass actor; do not grant a blanket GitHub Actions bypass and do not disable the rule.
- Probe both target repositories before expensive data collection begins. Distinguish persistent installation/permission denial from transient server or transport failure.
- Preserve bounded retries for replay-safe reads. Do not replay mutations unless their idempotency is explicit.
- Document credential rotation and installation expectations without exposing secret values.

## Contract Ledger

| Surface | Current contract | Required contract | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workflow credential boundary | Repository `GITHUB_TOKEN` is reused across repositories and publish | **Two** short-lived App tokens with explicit installations and explicit permission requests: Publisher (`contents: write`, `neo`) and Intake (`issues: write` + `metadata: read`, both DevIndex repos) | Focused workflow test plus permission preflight |
| Per-stage credential scope | Every stage inherits `process.env` wholesale | Each emission stage declares a `tokenScope`; the child env carries at most the one credential it is entitled to, and an undeclared scope fails closed | Unit assertions by VALUE across the whole child env |
| Git-layer credential | `persist-credentials` leaves the token in `.git/config` for the whole job | Checkout persists nothing; publisher auth supplied per-invocation via `GIT_CONFIG_*` in the child env, never argv | Argv witness at the `gitAuthenticated` boundary |
| `GitHub.query()` error classification | Integration denial enters the transient retry path | Persistent installation/permission denial fails fast; genuine transient reads remain bounded | Unit coverage for both classes |
| Ruleset `19087298` | No Data Sync bypass actor | Only the **Publisher** App may bypass for generated-data publication; the Intake identity cannot publish at all | Ruleset inspection plus controlled publish |

## Decision Record Impact

`none`. No ADR currently assigns Data Sync credential identity. This changes authorization and failure classification, not generated-content shape.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **Two** dedicated GitHub Apps are installed on their exact required repositories with documented minimal permissions — Publisher on `neo`, Intake on both DevIndex repositories.
- [ ] The workflow mints and uses short-lived installation tokens with explicitly requested permissions; cross-repository access no longer relies on the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
- [ ] Only the **Publisher** App is granted the narrow code-scanning-ruleset bypass needed for generated-data publication.
- [ ] Repository-access preflights run before expensive Data Sync stages and identify the failing repository/permission without leaking credentials.
- [ ] Persistent integration denial fails fast; transient, replay-safe reads retain bounded retry behavior.
- [ ] `[L3-deferred — operator handoff needed]` A controlled workflow proves that the Publisher App can publish a generated commit while the active ruleset remains enforced. **The read half is proven** (preflight-only run reached both DevIndex repos); the **publish half is not** — preflight-only stops before the push, so the bypass is configured but never exercised.
- [ ] Focused tests cover authentication classification and token plumbing.
- [ ] `[L3-deferred — operator handoff needed]` Three scheduled runs that reach these boundaries complete the OptIn read and generated-content push without an auth or ruleset terminal failure. Runtime-only: no pre-merge artifact can establish it.

## Out of Scope

- GraphQL quota budgeting and batch sizing
- Regeneration after `dev` advances during a run
- The Pages deployment PAT
- General GitHub 5xx availability
- Changing generated data or archive formats

## Avoided Traps

- No blanket bypass for every Actions workflow
- No ruleset disablement
- No long-lived, broadly scoped PAT
- No infinite retry of permanent authorization failures
- No reopening or mutating closed historical tickets

## Intake delta — live premise survives; one permission-topology fork precedes implementation

Fresh checks against current `dev`, the live ruleset, both DevIndex intake services, Neo KB, and GitHub’s current App-token contract preserve #15744’s core diagnosis after #15750:

- The workflow still passes the repository `GITHUB_TOKEN` through Data Sync, and the bounded publisher still performs `git push origin HEAD:dev` through the checkout credential.
- Ruleset `19087298` remains active with CodeQL protection and no bypass actor.
- #15750 moved publication out of inline YAML, but did not change either authorization boundary.

One required repository is missing from the ticket’s current framing: the scheduled sequence runs both OptIn **and OptOut**. `OptOut.mjs` reads `neomjs/devindex-opt-out` and mutates its issues by adding comments and closing processed requests, just as OptIn mutates `neomjs/devindex-opt-in`. A token installed only on `neo` plus `devindex-opt-in` would merely expose the next persistent integration denial later in the sequence.

There is also a real least-privilege fork. GitHub’s official `actions/create-github-app-token@v3` contract scopes a token with one repository set and one explicit permission set; it does not define a different permission map per selected repository. Therefore a single token spanning `neo`, `devindex-opt-in`, and `devindex-opt-out` would carry its aggregate `contents: write` and `issues: write` permissions across all three repositories. That is the minimum *aggregate* permission set for one App, but not strict per-repository least privilege. References: [official action token/repository/permission inputs](https://github.com/actions/create-github-app-token#inputs), [GitHub App installation permissions and selected repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/using-github-apps/installing-a-github-app-from-a-third-party).

### Recommendation

Use two purpose-scoped App identities/tokens within this same ticket:

1. **Publisher App** — installed only on `neomjs/neo`; owns the required Neo read permissions plus `contents: write`, supplies the checkout/push credential, and is the sole ruleset-bypass actor.
2. **Intake App** — installed only on `neomjs/devindex-opt-in` and `neomjs/devindex-opt-out`; owns `issues: write` and is injected only into the OptIn/OptOut child processes.

This keeps the ruleset-bypass identity unable to mutate the intake repositories and keeps the intake identity unable to publish to `neo`. The bounded publisher will need per-command environment injection rather than one global `GITHUB_TOKEN`; that is testable without exposing either secret.

Operator-owned decision before tracked implementation: accept the recommended two-App split, or explicitly accept the cross-repository overgrant of one aggregate-permission App. Once chosen, the open ticket can absorb the body delta; no new ticket or historical reopen is needed.

Architecture route: continue under #15744 ticket intake rather than an Ideation Sandbox, because this is a reversible workflow/credential split rather than a new subsystem. Blast class remains high operational/security due to secrets, three repository installations, and the ruleset bypass.

Delivers the preflight + classification half of #15744.

`Resource not accessible by integration` is returned for TWO conditions that share
one string: genuine GitHub-side flakiness, and a permanently missing App
installation. No message inspection separates them -- which is exactly why #15359
put the string in `retryableTransientErrorPatterns`, on real evidence of the same
token succeeding four hours later. That classification is correct for the flaky
case and catastrophic for the other: a permanent misconfiguration becomes an
unbounded series of identical retried failures, each looking like bad luck. This
pipeline spent eight days and sixty consecutive scheduled runs in that state.

The discriminator is not the message. It is WHEN the denial happens.

A probe issued before any collection, carrying no retry budget, cannot be
mid-batch flakiness -- it is the installation answering. A denial AFTER those
probes passed is the transient class the retry budget exists for. So the two ACs
that looked separate (preflight, and persistent-vs-transient classification) are
one design, and `retryableTransientErrorPatterns` is left untouched: weakening it
would break the flaky case #15359 documented with evidence.

The preflight names EVERY unreachable repository in one error rather than dying on
the first, so one fix round resolves both installations instead of discovering the
second only after correcting the first:

  [DataSync preflight] 2 required repository/repositories unreachable:
    - neomjs/devindex-opt-in (OptIn stargazer read): Resource not accessible by integration
    - neomjs/devindex-opt-out (OptOut issue read + close): Resource not accessible by integration
  This is a PERSISTENT authorization failure, not a transient read: ...
  Verify the intake App is installed on each repository above with `Issues: Read
  and write` and `Metadata: Read`.

`devindex-opt-out` is in the required set on @neo-gpt-emmy's catch: the scheduled
sequence runs OptOut as well as OptIn, so an installation covering only `neo` +
`devindex-opt-in` would pass a naive probe and fail one stage later -- after the
setup work already looked complete.

Two details the tests pin because getting either wrong reintroduces the outage:
the denial arrives as HTTP 200 with a body `errors` array, so reading
`response.status` alone reports the repository as reachable; and a NON-denial
failure must not be labelled persistent-authorization, or a network fault sends
the reader to the App settings. The classification has to be wrong-way-safe in
both directions, not only the loud one.

`preflight` is an injected seam on `emitGeneratedData`. Two existing specs began
failing once it landed -- correctly, since they call the emitter with no token.
They own stage ORDER, not access, so they stub the seam rather than the preflight
being weakened to accommodate them.

- 2026-07-26T00:54:01Z @neo-opus-ada referenced in commit `b7bc590` - "fix(build): the credential must not reach argv, and must not be printed if it does (#15744)

@neo-gpt-emmy found this on b15f5a77b3, and I introduced it two commits earlier
WHILE FIXING THE OTHER CREDENTIAL LEAK. Moving the Publisher token out of
.git/config (where persist-credentials left it for the whole job) and into a
`-c http.extraheader=...` ARGUMENT made it worse than config ever was.

Proven before fixing:

  error message leaks the header? true
  decodes to: x-access-token:ghs_SUPERSECRET123

argv is visible in `ps` to any process on the runner, and executeCommand
interpolates `args.join(' ')` into its failure message — so a failed push would
PRINT a working ruleset-bypass credential into a public CI log.

And base64 is not redaction. Actions masks the LITERAL secret string, so a
transformed secret does not match its own mask. The leak would have been plain,
decodable, and unmasked. That is also why the redaction below keys on SHAPE rather
than on a known value: masking cannot be the last line when a transform defeats it.

Two changes, primary and defence-in-depth:

1. The credential now travels through GIT_CONFIG_COUNT/_KEY_0/_VALUE_0 — git's own
   env-based config channel. Same effect as `-c`, no argv exposure, and scoped to
   the child process rather than written to .git/config where a later stage inherits
   it.

2. executeCommand redacts credential-shaped arguments from failure messages, so the
   next argv-borne secret is not printed even if one slips in. Asserted that ordinary
   arguments still appear: redaction must not blind the diagnostic it lives in.

credential; the run that was 'side-effect free').

Ninth finding on this PR, same shape as the other eight: a boundary where both sides

all three repos would let the ruleset-bypass identity mutate the intake repos and
let the intake identity publish here.

Each emission stage now declares a tokenScope, and scopedStageEnv builds its child
environment. The load-bearing detail is that it strips the SOURCE variables too,

one key:

  scope=none      sees-intake=false  sees-publisher=false  sees-ambient=false
  scope=intake    sees-intake=true   sees-publisher=FALSE  sees-ambient=false
  scope=publisher sees-intake=FALSE  sees-publisher=true   sees-ambient=false

tokenScope 'none' yields a child with no credential at all. A stage that turns out
to need one fails on its own missing-auth path rather than quietly succeeding on a
more privileged identity than it was granted; and a missing scoped token does not
fall back to ambient, which is how the single-token pipeline masked its boundary.

One existing spec pinned `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` on the run
step. The contract genuinely changed, so it now pins the two scoped variables plus

* feat(build): the denial that ran 60 times now fails in seconds and names the repo (#15744)

Delivers the preflight + classification half of #15744.

`Resource not accessible by integration` is returned for TWO conditions that share
one string: genuine GitHub-side flakiness, and a permanently missing App
installation. No message inspection separates them -- which is exactly why #15359
put the string in `retryableTransientErrorPatterns`, on real evidence of the same
token succeeding four hours later. That classification is correct for the flaky
case and catastrophic for the other: a permanent misconfiguration becomes an
unbounded series of identical retried failures, each looking like bad luck. This
pipeline spent eight days and sixty consecutive scheduled runs in that state.

The discriminator is not the message. It is WHEN the denial happens.

A probe issued before any collection, carrying no retry budget, cannot be
mid-batch flakiness -- it is the installation answering. A denial AFTER those
probes passed is the transient class the retry budget exists for. So the two ACs
that looked separate (preflight, and persistent-vs-transient classification) are
one design, and `retryableTransientErrorPatterns` is left untouched: weakening it
would break the flaky case #15359 documented with evidence.

the first, so one fix round resolves both installations instead of discovering the
second only after correcting the first:

  [DataSync preflight] 2 required repository/repositories unreachable:
    - neomjs/devindex-opt-in (OptIn stargazer read): Resource not accessible by integration
    - neomjs/devindex-opt-out (OptOut issue read + close): Resource not accessible by integration
  This is a PERSISTENT authorization failure, not a transient read: ...
  Verify the intake App is installed on each repository above with `Issues: Read
  and write` and `Metadata: Read`.

the denial arrives as HTTP 200 with a body `errors` array, so reading

failure must not be labelled persistent-authorization, or a network fault sends

both directions, not only the loud one.

required repository, and stops.

check that can only be performed by running them is a check nobody repeats while
iterating on an installation -- which is exactly when it is needed most. This one
is free to re-run, so a wrong installation can be corrected and re-verified in a
loop instead of one anxious shot.

setup steps. App installations are invisible to a non-admin token, and so are
ruleset bypass actors -- `bypass_actors` is omitted from the rulesets API below
admin, not returned empty. A dispatch is what turns "looks right in the UI" into
evidence.

The flag is opt-in on the EXACT string 'true'. A truthy-ish value short-circuiting
the pipeline would produce a scheduled run reporting success having done nothing,
which is the same silent-no-op class this ticket exists to remove -- so the spec
pins 'false', '1' and 'yes' as full runs.

Preflight failure still aborts in preflight-only mode; the mode skips collection,

Folds @neo-gpt-emmy's four-item blocker census. Two were already fixed at 894da5a918

claims the PR was making rather than gaps in what it built.

   `emitGeneratedData`, so control fell through to the publish path in
   `runDataSyncPipeline` and only stayed harmless because an empty emission stages
   no changes. That is a safety property borrowed from a coincidence: any future
   change making the publish path act on an unchanged tree turns a configuration
   check into a publication. It now exits the pipeline.

2. THE PREFLIGHT RETRIES, BOUNDED. This corrects the design argument, not an
   oversight. I claimed timing alone separated persistent from transient — a probe
   before any collection cannot be mid-batch flakiness. True, and insufficient: it
   does not rule out a flaky FIRST call. Declaring one denial permanently authorized
   because of WHEN it happened trades a permanent-misread-as-transient bug for a
   transient-misread-as-permanent one, and a scheduled run aborted on a single blip
   is its own outage.

   Persistence is now established by EXHAUSTION as well as timing. Fail-fast
   survives: three attempts resolve in seconds, and the case this exists for
   produced the same denial sixty consecutive times.

   I had explicitly rejected this in the PR body, under "where to push". Emmy
   pushed there.

3. APP-TOKEN PERMISSIONS ARE REQUESTED EXPLICITLY. Without `permission-*` inputs,
   v3 mints a token carrying every permission the installation holds. The Apps are
   scoped narrowly so the practical delta is small — but the least-privilege property
   then lives in a settings page nobody reads at review time, and widening an App
   silently widens its token. Publisher: contents write. Intake: issues write,
   metadata read, and explicitly no contents.

4. AN UNRECOGNISED tokenScope THROWS. `undefined` fell through to the `none` branch,
   so a stage added without one ran credential-less and looked deliberate. A spec
   comment claimed this made omission visible; nothing distinguished "declared none"
   from "forgot to declare". An undeclared scope is an unanswered question about
   which identity a stage is entitled to, not a default.

* fix(build): the credential must not reach argv, and must not be printed if it does (#15744)

@neo-gpt-emmy found this on b15f5a77b3, and I introduced it two commits earlier
WHILE FIXING THE OTHER CREDENTIAL LEAK. Moving the Publisher token out of
.git/config (where persist-credentials left it for the whole job) and into a
`-c http.extraheader=...` ARGUMENT made it worse than config ever was.

Proven before fixing:

  error message leaks the header? true
  decodes to: x-access-token:ghs_SUPERSECRET123

argv is visible in `ps` to any process on the runner, and executeCommand
interpolates `args.join(' ')` into its failure message — so a failed push would
PRINT a working ruleset-bypass credential into a public CI log.

And base64 is not redaction. Actions masks the LITERAL secret string, so a
transformed secret does not match its own mask. The leak would have been plain,
decodable, and unmasked. That is also why the redaction below keys on SHAPE rather
than on a known value: masking cannot be the last line when a transform defeats it.

Two changes, primary and defence-in-depth:

1. The credential now travels through GIT_CONFIG_COUNT/_KEY_0/_VALUE_0 — git's own
   env-based config channel. Same effect as `-c`, no argv exposure, and scoped to
   the child process rather than written to .git/config where a later stage inherits
   it.

2. executeCommand redacts credential-shaped arguments from failure messages, so the
   next argv-borne secret is not printed even if one slips in. Asserted that ordinary
   arguments still appear: redaction must not blind the diagnostic it lives in.

repository, and the Publisher App holds `contents` while labels are `issues`

already present in the job under `permissions:` — so this widens an existing

* docs(build): correct a falsified claim about create-github-app-token (#17150)

An earlier revision of this comment asserted that `create-github-app-token`
"fails the step outright when asked for a permission the installation lacks",
and used that to argue revoking `contents` would take the pipeline down before it
could emit a corpus.

Falsified by measurement. Run 31877595849 requested `permission-deployments:
write` -- a permission `neomjs-devindex-intake` does not hold -- and the mint
step SUCCEEDED. The action does not validate requested permissions against the
installation.

Two consequences, both worse to leave standing than to correct:

- The operational warning was overstated. Revoking `contents` degrades the
  stargazer read (which #17148's deferral now absorbs), it does not kill the mint
  and freeze the corpus. The coupling between this line and the App grant is
  real; the failure mode is not.

- A successful mint proves NOTHING about what the token carries. #17150's probe
  matrix leaned on mint-success as conclusive evidence that `administration:
  read` was genuinely held. That inference is void. The matrix's CONCLUSIONS
  survive -- they rest on the capability probe (stargazers reachable / denied),
  which is a direct observation -- but the corroborating argument does not, and
  the ticket is corrected to say so.

* docs(build): restore the true coupling claim -- my correction was the false one (#17150)

Reverting f5ce78fe4a's correction. It asserted `create-github-app-token` does not
validate requested permissions, citing run 31877595849 as a success. The raw log
of that run says otherwise:

  ##[error]The permissions requested are not granted to this installation.

The step FAILED. I read `conclusion` from the jobs API, which `continue-on-error`
rewrites to `success` on a failed step -- and #17162's guard was present on that
probe branch. So the guard rewrote the field I used to judge whether the guard
was needed.

Consequence for the operator warning, restored to the stronger form: revoking
`contents` on the App while this line remains does not merely cost the stargazer
read, it fails the mint outright."

connection-selecting probe, without which the preflight would report `reachable`
